conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ve reviewed your chart and want to go over why you’re here. You came in with fever and abdominal pain after accessing your port, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I do my weekly port flush at home, and this time the fluid looked milky, even though I haven’t used TPN in months. Then I spiked a fever—102.7—and had chills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. We also saw your blood pressure was very high when you arrived—was that unusual for you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, really high. I usually run low. The nurse who visited me thought it might be stress or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Given your history with Crohn’s and past port infections, we’re worried this could be a bloodstream infection from the port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I’ve had that before with coagulase-negative staph. Do we know if it’s that now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve drawn blood cultures. If it’s growing, we’ll know in a day or two. Until then, we’re starting IV vancomycin to cover that exact bug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to vancomycin, though. I break out in rashes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that in your chart—multiple antibiotic allergies. But we believe the benefit outweighs the risk right now. We’ll monitor you closely and have Benadryl ready if a reaction occurs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I trust you. What about my belly pain? It’s been worse the last two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. You’ve had so many surgeries, it’s hard to tell if it’s Crohn’s flare, a partial blockage, or something else. We’ve ordered a CT scan to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also threw up once. And I’ve had this lip thing since this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noticed a small lesion on your lower right lip. It doesn’t look like a typical cold sore. But given your history, we’ll watch it. Could be herpes simplex.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures from yesterday are negative so far, which is reassuring, but we’ll keep checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet ruled out. It can take up to 48 hours to grow. We’re still treating as if it’s a port-related infection because of your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m still nauseous and my belly feels full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray showed a distended colon. We’re placing a nasogastric tube to help decompress your stomach and relieve nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate those tubes. But if it helps, okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. No bowel obstruction, which is great. But there’s mild thickening in your sigmoid colon—likely Crohn’s inflammation. No strictures seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not a blockage? That’s good. But why the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Inflammation can cause pain even without a stricture. We’re working with GI to plan a colonoscopy to look more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No indication yet. We’re managing this medically. Your NG tube is helping—output has decreased.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest blood cultures are still negative. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I still feel weak. And I noticed I’m more pale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped, so we’re giving a unit of packed red cells today to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I’ve been anemic for years. Is it worse now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely from chronic blood loss and poor absorption. We’ll keep monitoring and supplement iron when you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All blood cultures over the past 48 hours are negative. That suggests the infection is responding to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We still need to address your abdominal pain and rule out other issues. Also, we’ve noticed a patch on your chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Chest? I don’t have a cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, but there’s a faint opacity in your right upper lobe. Could be atelectasis or early pneumonia. We’ll treat it as possible pneumonia just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fever’s gone, and you’re feeling better. We’re going to try removing the NG tube today if your belly stays soft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. Can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids and see how you tolerate it. Your gut has been sluggish, so we’ll go slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You kept down broth and juice—great. We’re advancing to soft foods. Also, the chest X-ray shows the opacity is getting denser. We’re adding antibiotics for pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I feel fine. No cough, no shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes infections don’t cause symptoms, especially with your medical history. Better to treat it early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All recent blood cultures are negative. We’re confident the port infection is under control. We’re keeping the port because of your difficult access history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I don’t want another surgery for access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for a colonoscopy today. It’s limited due to your anatomy, but we want to rule out any active Crohn’s inflammation or stricture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they find something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hard to say. The CT showed mild changes, but colonoscopy gives a direct view. We’ll know more afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colonoscopy was limited but showed no major strictures or active ulcers. We’re following up with a barium enema for a better view of the colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another test? I’m tired of this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s exhausting. But we want to be sure there’s no narrowing that could cause problems later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The barium enema is back—no stricture in the sigmoid. The study was limited because you weren’t fully prepped, but we didn’t see anything concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my pain isn’t from a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. It’s likely from chronic inflammation and motility issues. We’re focusing on symptom management and bowel regimen now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pneumonia appears to be stabilizing. The chest X-ray shows no worsening. We’ll continue antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All blood and urine cultures are negative. You’ve completed two weeks of IV vancomycin. We’re switching to oral antibiotics for a short course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m cured?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infection is treated. We’ll keep monitoring. You’re tolerating food well, and your pain is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’re being discharged tomorrow. We’ll send you home with a short course of oral antibiotics and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need blood work in a few days—CBC, chem panel, TSH. And keep your GI and primary care appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my lip? It’s not going away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll treat it as herpes simplex. Use the antiviral cream and let your doctor know if it spreads.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Vital signs are normal, you’re eating, and your pain is minimal. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, so ready. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: call if you spike a fever, have vomiting, or new pain. Keep up with your labs and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And flush the port regularly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, per protocol. And watch for redness or discharge. Otherwise, rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my anxiety’s been worse here. The hospital setting… it brings back bad memories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I remember your PTSD history. We’ve noted that. Your primary care can help with counseling or medication if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d appreciate that. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your well-being matters. Let’s get you home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and meds shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Proud of how you’ve handled everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Means a lot. I was really scared at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. But you’re through the worst of it. Keep building on this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your outpatient team to ensure smooth follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest up, take your meds, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with abdominal pain and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The pain came on suddenly this morning. I’ve had Crohn’s for years, and this feels like one of my flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You had a fever earlier too, around 100.5. Any cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no breathing issues. But I did vomit a few times, and I’ve had chills the past couple days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The CT scan didn’t show a blockage or new abscess. Your bowel wall thickening is stable. We think this is likely a Crohn’s flare with possible ileus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been off pain meds for a while, feeling stable, but last week the fevers started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting IV antibiotics—cipro and flagyl—for now, just in case there’s infection. We’ll also keep you NPO and use the NG tube to help with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I placed the NG tube myself in the ER so I could get the CT. It’s uncomfortable, but I know it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was smart. We’ll reassess your pain and see if we can ease up on the dilaudid. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative, which is great—no active bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My port’s been okay—no redness or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your CRP and ESR are elevated, which supports inflammation, likely from Crohn’s. Stool tests were negative for C. diff and other infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection, just a flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the current thought. But your chest X-ray shows pneumonia in the right lung. Could be from aspiration when you vomited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I didn’t even feel like I was coughing it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can happen silently. We’re switching your antibiotic from cipro to levofloxacin to better cover pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will I need more scans?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll repeat the chest X-ray in a few days to check the pneumonia. For now, focus on resting and letting your gut rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. The new chest X-ray shows the pneumonia is still there, but your oxygen levels are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been afebrile since yesterday. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My nausea’s still there, but less than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the NG tube for now. GI wants to do a colonoscopy soon to check your bowel health before considering new Crohn’s meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d prefer to wait for my regular GI doctor. I don’t want just anyone doing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll coordinate with your GI. In the meantime, we’re keeping you on IV fluids and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed contamination, so no UTI. Blood cultures still negative—great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not another infection. My port’s been trouble before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring it closely. No signs of infection there. Your hemoglobin dropped a bit, but it’s stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had iron deficiency for years. I just can’t tolerate oral iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue monitoring. For now, we’re not planning a transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been passing gas and have some bowel sounds. That’s a sign your ileus is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I might be ready to try a little food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids and see how you do. If that goes well, we can advance to a soft diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the BRAT diet well yesterday. We’re going to remove the NG tube this morning if you’re okay with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Please. I’m tired of it. My nausea’s much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it now. Let us know if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the pneumonia is starting to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel stronger every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also restarting your citalopram for anxiety. You mentioned PTSD gets worse in hospitals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s hard. I had a bad experience years ago. I declined psych consult, but I’ll take the Celexa.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve also prescribed PRN valium if you feel overwhelmed. Social work checked in with you yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she was very kind. I’m okay for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The latest chest X-ray shows continued improvement in the pneumonia. Your lungs are clearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I haven’t had any fever in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll finish the IV antibiotics soon. Now, about the colonoscopy—your GI doctor scheduled it for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Finally. I want to make sure it’s him.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is. He’ll assess for strictures and inflammation. It’ll help decide if you can start a new Crohn’s medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colonoscopy was done. Prep wasn’t ideal, but they saw no strictures or major inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no blockages?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. That’s good. But because the view wasn’t perfect, they’ll want a repeat when you’re fully recovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure I prep better next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you with that. For now, you’re doing well. You’ve been on a soft diet, and your pain is controlled with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll go home on oral cipro and metronidazole for 10 more doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have some tablets for breakthrough pain, but we encourage tapering off quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to stay on them. I’ve been off before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll also send you home with benadryl and Phenergan for nausea, if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my port care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue flushing per protocol. We’re concerned about future access, but your surgeon is aware.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your pain and nausea are much better, and your pneumonia is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. Thank you for listening to me about my GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Follow up with your PCP and GI. Call if you develop fever, worsening pain, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll restart my Celexa daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your instructions are printed. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you to your ride in about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your B12 and thyroid meds should continue as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t missed those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep up with the pantoprazole for stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call you in a few days to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ride is here. Take care and get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand when to call the doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if I get fever, pain, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve had swelling in my face for about a week, and it’s getting worse. Also, when I flushed my port the other day, I felt sharp pain in my right upper belly that went up to my eye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any other symptoms—fever, shortness of breath, nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chills. I’ve had mild nausea and threw up once this morning. No diarrhea. But I’ve been more short of breath lately, especially lying down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of SVC syndrome and Crohn’s, we need to check for a few things. We’ve ordered a CT scan to look for a clot and to evaluate your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared. Last time I had facial swelling, it was a clot. And I need my pain meds—I usually take Dilaudid every few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted your usual medications, including Dilaudid, and we’ll manage your pain safely. We also know about your PTSD and will make sure you’re as comfortable as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT results are back. There’s a clot in your superior vena cava extending toward the right atrium. That explains the facial swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is it dangerous? Do I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The vascular team reviewed it. Because you have good collateral veins, it’s not an emergency. Surgery isn’t recommended right now. But we need to treat the clot with blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had HIT before. I can’t take heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re starting you on Argatroban, a different blood thinner that’s safe with HIT. We’ll switch to Coumadin later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better. What about my belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows stable changes from your Crohn’s—some thickening near your old surgical site. No obstruction. GI thinks this could be a flare, so we’re starting Cipro to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to Cipro. I thought that was in my chart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right—it is. I apologize. We’ll switch to a different antibiotic that’s safe for you. Let me correct that order.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve changed your antibiotic to one you’re not allergic to. Your pain is still bothering you, so we’re giving IV Dilaudid and Benadryl, which also helps with anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. The Benadryl helps me relax. Can I have my Valium too? I get really anxious in hospitals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve ordered Oxazepam, which is similar. You can have it as needed. We want to keep you calm and comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative—no infection. Urine and stool tests also show no concerning bacteria or C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pain isn’t from an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not that we can see. It still looks like a Crohn’s flare. We’ll continue the new antibiotic and monitor your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the clot? Is it getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re treating it. Argatroban is working. We’ll check your INR today to see when we can safely switch to Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now therapeutic. We’ve stopped Argatroban and are continuing Coumadin. You’ll need regular blood tests after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to go to a lab every week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, initially. You have a follow-up with the anticoagulation clinic next week. They’ll help manage your dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your facial swelling is improving. That’s a good sign the blood thinner is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can feel it’s less tight. My belly pain is better too. Can I eat more than just broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll advance your diet to soft foods. Given your short bowel syndrome, we’ll go slow to avoid discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ve been on TPN before, but I’m glad I can eat now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. Your hemoglobin has dropped a bit, but it’s stable now. No need for transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your echo was normal—no clot in the heart, good heart function. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that. What about my port? Can I use it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the clot is stable and you’re on a good blood thinner. Your port can be used again, but we’ll keep it flushed properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do a 10% ethanol lock weekly. Should I keep doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’ll send you home with instructions to continue that to prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Coumadin—three 1mg tablets daily. The dose may change, so follow up with the clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have Dilaudid tablets for five days, just in case. Use Tramadol if you need something milder. And keep taking Cipro for the full two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my anxiety meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Citalopram and Oxazepam as needed. We lowered the Citalopram dose slightly due to your TSH being high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My thyroid? I take Levothyroxine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your TSH is elevated, so we’re keeping your dose the same for now. Follow up with your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR this morning is 3.1—perfect. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved. Any warning signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Return if you have face swelling again, shortness of breath, chest pain, fevers, or bloody diarrhea. Also, if you fall or hit your head, come in—warfarin increases bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’re stable, pain is controlled, and labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Will I need help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should be fine. You’re walking well and eating. Just take it easy the first few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to keep my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with GI, the anticoagulation clinic, and your primary doctor. We’ll send all the records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my port care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the ethanol lock as before. If you have redness or pain at the site, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you home with a plan. Take your meds, rest, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You came in last night with severe right thigh pain and some facial swelling. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Two weeks ago, I was discharged after being treated for facial swelling from my port clot. Yesterday, I was flushing my port and felt sudden pain from my chest to my back. I went to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And then they tried to place a line in your groin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They tried both sides, multiple times. It was awful. Then they realized one port was still working, so they stopped. But later that day, my right leg started throbbing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The ultrasound shows a large hematoma near your right femoral vessels, but no blood clot. It’s likely from the needle attempts while you were on warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a DVT? But my leg is so tight and painful. I can barely move it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No DVT. The blood flow in your veins is normal. The hematoma is pressing on nerves, which explains the pain and the numbness down your leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fever? I had 101.2 at the other ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about infection, but your blood cultures are pending. We’ve started you on dicloxacillin as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to so many antibiotics. Is this one safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, dicloxacillin is not on your allergy list. We’re monitoring closely. We also saw slight facial swelling—were you still on warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. My INR was 5 a few days ago, so I stopped warfarin. I was supposed to restart it later for my port change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That explains the facial swelling. Your SVC might be clotting again. We’ll need to restart anticoagulation carefully because of the hematoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what will you use? I can’t take heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Because of your HIT antibodies, we’ll start argatroban. It works quickly and can be stopped fast if the hematoma worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain? It’s still really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving IV Dilaudid and Benadryl for nausea. We’ll keep adjusting until it’s under control. Surgery and vascular teams agree no drainage is needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been so anxious. The hospital triggers my PTSD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. We’ve continued your citalopram and will use oxazepam as needed. We’ll keep your room quiet and give you space when needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your hemoglobin dropped to 22.2 but is now rising. No transfusion needed. We’ll send you home with B12 and discuss IV iron with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. The anemia is from blood loss into the hematoma. It’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture grew Klebsiella, but it’s likely a contaminant. Repeat culture showed no growth. We’ll stop antibiotics after 10 days if no other source is found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t have a UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. No symptoms, and the repeat test was clean. We’ll watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The follow-up ultrasound shows no change in the hematoma size. That’s actually good—it’s not expanding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it’s not getting smaller either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, but these take time. The priority is managing pain and preventing new clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your facial swelling is worsening. We need to fix your port and SVC blockage. Interventional radiology will do a procedure tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What will they do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll reopen the SVC with a balloon and clean the clot off your port—called 'port stripping.' You’ll be under anesthesia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it help the swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Once blood flows freely, the swelling should go down. After that, we’ll restart warfarin with a fondaparinux bridge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure was successful. They reopened your SVC and cleaned the fibrin sheath off your port. Both ports are now working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to ensure the anticoagulation is stable. We’ve started fondaparinux and low-dose warfarin. Target INR is 2.5–3.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the argatroban?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped it. Now that your SVC is open, we can safely transition back to warfarin with the bridge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.6. That’s in range. You’ll continue fondaparinux for two more days after it stabilizes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then just the warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Long-term. We’ve lowered the dose to 2 mg daily to avoid another high INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is better. We’re switching you to an oral Dilaudid taper to avoid withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on so much IV pain medicine. I’m worried about getting off it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The taper is designed to ease that. You’ll take decreasing doses over five days, then return to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my port? I was using ethanol flushes, but they made me feel awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting ethanol flushes at home. They help prevent clots, but we’ll monitor how you tolerate them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is now 24.5—still low but improving. Facial swelling is gone. Hematoma is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I walk more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as tolerated. The numbness is improving. No signs of nerve damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge tomorrow. You’ll go home on warfarin, fondaparinux for five days, and the Dilaudid taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check INR on the 16th. Continue fondaparinux for two days after it’s therapeutic. See your PCP to discuss IV iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the swelling comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go to the ER immediately if you have trouble breathing or swallowing. Same if leg numbness returns or worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the anxiety? Being in the hospital was hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with oxazepam as needed. Your citalopram continues. Please reach out if PTSD symptoms flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable. We’ve faxed prescriptions to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s been a lot, but I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Remember: take the taper as directed, check your INR, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m ready to be home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged home services for nursing support. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Call us with any questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your progress through your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to focus on healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’re well on your way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy these next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with high fevers and right thigh pain—can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was home and started feeling really sick—fever, chills, nausea. My thigh pain came back, right where the old hematoma was.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were just discharged two weeks ago after that hematoma and the SVC procedure. Any facial swelling this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not this time. Just the fever and the pain. It scared me—I didn’t know if it was serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re going to check things out. We’ve already done blood work and a chest X-ray. The X-ray looks clear—no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. But why the fever? I was fine at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. Could be infection, inflammation, or even a flare of your Crohn’s. We’ll keep monitoring and run more tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the thigh pain? Is the hematoma back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We ordered an ultrasound. It should help us see if there’s a new hematoma or something else going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is back. Good news—the old hematoma is completely gone. No sign of it in the groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does my thigh still hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we’re trying to figure out. The pain could be from muscle strain, nerve irritation, or a small new bleed. We’ll keep watching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been vomiting too—green stuff. That’s not normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bilious vomiting. That’s concerning. Could mean your stomach isn’t emptying well. We might need a CT scan to check your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the CT scan. Your colon looks okay—no Crohn’s flare or blockage. But there’s a small fluid collection in your right thigh.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it another hematoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It’s small—about 3 cm. Not like the big one before. We’ll watch it, but it doesn’t need surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vomiting? Is it from my Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of obstruction or Crohn’s flare on the scan. More likely gastric dysmotility—your stomach isn’t moving food well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you here for a few days. We’ve placed an NG tube to help your stomach rest and reduce vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The NG tube is working. You’re not vomiting as much. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but the Dilaudid helps. I’m just tired of being in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re watching you closely. Your fever hasn’t returned, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are stable. White count was a bit high yesterday but is improving. No infection found in blood cultures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the fever was just a one-time thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks that way. Sometimes fevers happen without a clear cause, especially with complex medical histories like yours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Crohn’s? Is it acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The CT showed no inflammation, strictures, or fistulas. Your Crohn’s seems quiet right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try removing the NG tube today. Your stomach seems to be moving better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. I hate this tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips. If you keep them down, we’ll slowly increase. But if you vomit, we might need it back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight—no vomiting. We’ll advance your diet to soft foods today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How’s my thigh?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The small fluid area is stable. It’s likely resolving on its own. Pain should improve with time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds? I’m on so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your thyroid, vitamin, and Crohn’s meds. We’ll adjust the Dilaudid and Benadryl with a taper plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Taper? Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To avoid withdrawal. You’ve been on them for pain and nausea. We’ll slowly reduce the dose so your body adjusts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. You’ve kept down solid food, no vomiting. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the Dilaudid taper as written—start every 4 hours as needed, then slowly space it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Benadryl shot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get injections at first, then taper to oral. We’ll send supplies home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my port? Do I still need to flush it with alcohol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily with 10% ethanol to prevent infections, especially with your history. Then flush with saline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. Keep up with your PCP appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so anxious coming in, but you’ve been great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here for you. Call if you have chest pain, bloody vomit, or trouble breathing. Otherwise, rest and follow the taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your warfarin dose stays the same. Keep monitoring INR with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And take calcium with vitamin D as before. Your levels were low, so it’s important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over discharge papers and meds. You’re cleared to leave by 1 PM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one more thing—should I worry about the fever coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unlikely. If it does, or if pain worsens, call your doctor. But right now, you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using the oxazepam if anxiety flares. Hospital stays can be tough with your PTSD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been hard. But I feel safer going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ve noted that in your record so future teams are aware.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re strong—you’ve been through a lot. Now focus on healing at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with fevers—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had fevers up to 102, with chills, for about three weeks. I finished a course of cipro for a UTI, but the fevers didn’t go away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned pelvic pain and pain in your inner thighs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been a dull ache, radiating down. I also noticed blood and air in my urine and stool a week ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ve reviewed your records. You had blood cultures at the other hospital that grew Bacillus species. That’s likely why the fevers are persisting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve had port infections before, but this doesn’t feel the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right. Your port is flushing well, and there’s no redness or tenderness. So it’s probably not a port infection this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We ordered a CT scan to check for fistulas or abscesses. The first one didn’t show any bowel issues, but we saw a new lung nodule and mild splenomegaly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Splenomegaly? I’ve never had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s new. We’re not sure why yet. Could be from infection or something else. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did more blood work. Your white count is low, and we’ve started you on IV vancomycin and Zosyn based on the Bacillus finding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that clear the infection? I’ve been so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. We’re treating it aggressively. But we still need to find the source of the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a fall yesterday, didn’t you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I put lotion on my feet and slipped. My arm hurts, but I didn’t hit my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: X-ray shows no fracture. Just soft tissue injury. We’ll keep an eye on it. Please wear booties next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Big update. Your pelvic MRI came back. You have a small abscess—about 6x9x18 mm—in your right pectineus muscle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An abscess? In my muscle? How did that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure. It’s not connected to your bowel or your old hematoma. But it’s likely the source of your fevers and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics should help it go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since it’s small, we’re treating it with IV antibiotics rather than draining it. We’ll repeat the MRI as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My pain has been worse in that area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures are negative. That’s a good sign—the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my anemia? I’ve been feeling weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin is low, and your iron studies confirm iron deficiency. We’ll give you IV ferric gluconate today and a B12 shot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been on iron pills before, but they upset my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. With your short bowel, absorption is poor. IV is better for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelets dropped a bit, likely from the Zosyn. We’ve stopped it, and they’re already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this level. We caught it early. Your counts are stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been afebrile for two days. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Still some pain, but less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on IV vancomycin. We’ll switch to oral pain meds soon and start a taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urine culture was negative. No C. diff. EBV and CMV tests suggest old infection, not active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the abscess is really the main issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Everything points to the pectineus abscess as the source of your bacteremia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another CT to check if the abscess has changed. It’s not clearly visible, which may mean it’s responding to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. We’ll still need a follow-up MRI to be sure it’s resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was low yesterday—1.9. We held coumadin and gave fondaparinux for two days because of your SVC syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always have trouble with my blood thinners. My gut doesn’t absorb them well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Today your INR is 3.9—slightly high. So you’ll take only 2 mg of coumadin tonight instead of 5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch for bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish three more days of IV vancomycin at home. A nurse will help you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll start a taper on dilaudid and benadryl—both by mouth. I’ll give you the schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Outpatient pelvic MRI in a few weeks with sedation. Blood cultures two weeks after discharge. And your PCP will check your INR tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my iron and B12?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your supplements. We’ve adjusted your calcium and vitamin D too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s discharge day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Just to confirm—I take 2 mg of coumadin tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Then back to 4 or 5 mg depending on your INR. Your clinic will call you to adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I spike a fever again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER if you have fever over 101, worsening pain, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in this morning feeling unwell. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I finished my vancomycin course three days ago, and I was doing okay, but then two nights ago I had a low fever. Last night was terrible—I was up all night with severe back and groin pain, couldn’t sleep, and started vomiting this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your heart rate was elevated when you arrived. We drew blood cultures from your port and started some fluids. You mentioned you tried your pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took my usual dilaudid, but it didn’t help much. I added tramadol and that helped a little, but not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re going to keep you on IV dilaudid for now, with benadryl to help with any nausea. We’ll monitor your symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m worried—could this be the infection coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid concern. Your blood cultures so far show no growth, which is reassuring. But we’re not ruling anything out yet. We’ll repeat them and check your urine and stool as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is clear, and your NG tube is in the right place. Your port tip is in the SVC, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many scans and tubes… it brings back bad memories from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll keep things as calm as possible. We’re here to help you through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat urine culture came back positive for Klebsiella. That could explain the fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Klebsiella? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a common bacteria that can cause UTIs. We’re starting you on ciprofloxacin to treat it. It’s important you finish the full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I thought my last infection was from the abscess?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was Bacillus cereus from the pectineus abscess. That abscess is improving, but we’re being cautious. Since you just finished antibiotics, we want to make sure nothing’s lingering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling an MRI of your pelvis today to check on the abscess. We also need to rule out endocarditis, so we’ll do a transesophageal echo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another MRI? I hope it’s not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The preliminary report says the abscess is smaller—only 3 mm now. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI is back. The abscess is definitely shrinking—no new collections. But we saw something incidental: a small 8 mm spot in your right femur. It looks like an enchondroma—benign bone tumor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A tumor? Even if it’s benign, that sounds scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But enchondromas are common and usually harmless. We’ll have a radiology specialist confirm, and you’ll follow up as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your TEE was normal—no sign of endocarditis. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the heart is okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no vegetations or clots. Your valves look structurally normal. We’re confident the infection hasn’t spread there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a huge relief. What about restarting antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infectious disease recommends restarting IV vancomycin for another two weeks. Even though the abscess is better, we want to be thorough given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was hoping to avoid more IV meds. But if it’s needed, I’ll do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll arrange home infusion. You’ll get it twice daily for 14 days. We’ll also send you home with cipro for the UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count dropped to 2.4. It’s been low before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been low in past admissions. Hematology said it’s likely related to my Crohn’s or meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll monitor it. Hematology wants a recheck in three days after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your blood cultures are negative. That’s good—we’re not seeing active bacteremia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the vancomycin is working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s preventive at this point. We’re making sure we don’t have a relapse. Your CRP and ESR are still elevated, so there’s inflammation, but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having trouble urinating. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely from the pain meds and your history. We’ve been monitoring. You’re improving—no catheter needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your heart today—just a quick check. Everything looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that different from the TEE?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this was a surface echo—less detailed but good for checking heart function. Your ejection fraction is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been afebrile for over 24 hours. That’s a big step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge on Thursday. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled and your IV meds are set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. But I’m nervous about managing everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a nurse to help set up your vancomycin. And your dilaudid will be on a taper—starting every 4 hours, then slowing down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We adjusted your warfarin dose. You’ll now take 2 mg five times a week and 4 mg twice a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was trending high. With your short bowel, absorption varies. This schedule should keep it more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you remind me about the follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll have labs twice weekly—CBC, chem7, INR, and vancomycin troughs. Send them to Infectious Disease. And follow up with radiology about the enchondroma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the MRI for the abscess?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have an outpatient MRI in a few weeks under sedation to check for full resolution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking about the pain. It’s better, but still there. Is it from the abscess or something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abscess is healing, but you have chronic pain from fibromyalgia and Crohn’s. The groin pain may also be referred from the muscle inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. Keep up with your meds, rest, and follow up. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re afebrile, stable, and your pain is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m so glad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember: finish both antibiotics—vancomycin for 14 days, cipro for 7. Watch for fever, pain, or swelling. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll schedule the labs and MRI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take care of yourself, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I be worried about the enchondroma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. It’s likely benign. Just get it checked as recommended. If it grows or causes pain, we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The discharge nurse will go over your meds and instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will my Crohn’s be checked soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your GI follow-up is scheduled. We don’t think it’s active now, but we’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had so many surgeries—I just want to stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. You’ve been through a lot, but you’re managing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my iron? I’ve been anemic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low but stable. We didn’t give IV iron this time, but we’ll check it at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch for fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and eat iron-rich foods. We’ll adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my anxiety gets worse in hospitals. Is there support for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Your mental health is important. Your psychiatrist is on your team. Please reach out if you’re struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here for you. Now go home, rest, and heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been having really bad headaches for about a week—frontal, both sides. And I’ve been vomiting five times a day for the last four days. Just clear, no blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, low-grade fevers—around 100°F the past three nights. No chills. I’ve also had watery diarrhea a few times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any confusion or balance issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—five days ago, I had trouble finding words. My husband noticed. And I felt off-balance walking. But it passed by the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. You also mentioned tinnitus and light sensitivity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, ringing in my ears one morning and the lights hurt. But that’s better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Your PCP found your INR was 7.3—very high. That’s why we’re holding your warfarin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried about bleeding. No bruising or bleeding though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that. We’re ordering an MRI of your head to rule out any bleeding or infection, given the headaches and high INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that common with high INR? I’ve had Crohn’s and infections before, but not this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s precautionary. With your history of bacteremia and recent antibiotics, we want to be sure there’s no brain abscess or bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your brain MRI came back. No bleeding, no abscess, no stroke. Just a small old spot in the frontal lobe—unchanged from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. So the headaches aren’t dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not from a structural issue. Neurology thinks it could be related to your recent illness or even tension. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been nauseous and bloated. I put in an NG tube at home to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that on the X-ray. We removed it because it was pulling out your food. We’ll manage the nausea with meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wanted relief. My gut’s been off since all the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re starting you on Flagyl for possible bacterial overgrowth. It should help the diarrhea and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the nausea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since yesterday morning. Still bloated, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re also repleting your potassium and magnesium—both were low, likely from the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always run low on potassium. Is that from Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and with short bowel syndrome, absorption is tough. We’re giving IV and oral supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pelvic MRI shows the old abscess in your right thigh muscle is healing well—just a small area of inflammation left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. And the small bone lesion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still there—a small enchondroma in your hip. Stable. No need to treat, just follow up as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noticed some spotting and itching down there. And I feel air coming out sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an exam with a nurse. There’s mild skin splitting and redness—likely a yeast infection. No fistula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve worried about fistulas for years. But if you’re sure…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GYN agrees—no signs of a rectovaginal fistula. We’ll start Monistat for the yeast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your right arm has mild swelling. Given your SVC syndrome, we did an ultrasound—no clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get that sometimes. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. The veins show changes from your past SVC narrowing, but no DVT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been anxious—especially with male staff. It brings back bad memories.
