conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted your PTSD. We’ll use female staff when possible. Your Celexa and Valium are helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I feel safer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed a cough and low fevers. Chest X-ray shows pneumonia in the right lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? How? I haven’t been around sick people.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s from aspirating stomach contents—maybe during vomiting or with the NG tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So it’s not contagious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We’re adding levofloxacin to your Flagyl for coverage. You’re not contagious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I need to stay longer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a few more days. We want to make sure the infection clears and you can take the antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your INR is now 2.1—back in the safe range. We’re restarting your warfarin tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I was worried about clots with my SVC history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep using the ethanol lock in your port to prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No more headaches, vomiting, or fevers. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish a 7-day course of Flagyl and levofloxacin at home. And 3 more days of Monistat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your usual dose—2 mg five times a week, 4 mg twice a week. Keep your INR checks with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the iron infusion I got?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for your chronic anemia. Follow up with your doctor about more if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on so many antibiotics. Will my gut ever recover?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s tough with your history. But we’re hopeful the Flagyl helps reset your gut flora. Probiotics later might help too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if you develop fever, worsening cough, or confusion. Otherwise, follow up with your PCP in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling good. Headache’s gone, and I’ve eaten two meals without nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Keep up with your meds and rest. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your vaginal symptoms. If the itching returns, let your doctor know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. The Monistat helped a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And remember, no driving while on Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I’ll have my husband help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. All set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand the pneumonia antibiotics are for 7 days, even if you feel better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll finish them all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. And call if you cough up blood or have trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel strong enough to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re ready. We’re discharging you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—any dizziness or weakness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m steady on my feet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re cleared to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick call to confirm you got home okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, home and resting. Thank you for checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I know you just got here—how are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not great. I had this weird tingling in my right arm yesterday, then swelling. It went away, but then I started seeing blue lights and got a terrible headache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned some nausea and vomiting too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I felt like my speech was slurred for a bit. I called EMS. They said the CT was normal, but I’m still worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT didn’t show any stroke or bleeding, which is reassuring. We’ll keep monitoring you. You also had low potassium and magnesium—we’re giving IV replacements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those issues before. It’s from my Crohn’s and short gut. But this headache—it’s different. Throbbing, on the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That, plus the visual changes, makes us think it could be a migraine. Your sister has them too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she does. But I’m also running a fever now. Could that be from something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’re checking blood cultures to rule out infection. Given your port-a-cath and history, we need to be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound on your right arm for the swelling. No blood clot found, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That tingling and bumps are gone now, but I still feel off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures flagged early. We’re seeing gram-positive rods. Could be Bacillus species. We’ve started antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve had line infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be. We’re treating it seriously. Because you spiked a fever, we’re also concerned about meningitis, so we’ll do a lumbar puncture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like needles. Is it really necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But with your symptoms and fever, we need to rule out infection in the spinal fluid. It’s a quick procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the spinal fluid showed no infection. No white cells, no bacteria. That rules out meningitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. But I still feel nauseated and bloated. Is it my Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your CT scan didn’t show any abscess or bowel blockage. The GI team thinks it’s a flare-up with ileus. We’ll keep managing symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t take Zofran or Reglan. I’m allergic. Benadryl and Dilaudid help, but I know you’re cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use Benadryl for nausea. For pain, we’ll stick to your home Dilaudid, but we’ll plan a taper to avoid dependency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood culture confirmed Bacillus cereus. It’s sensitive to levofloxacin, so we’re switching from IV vancomycin to oral levofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the infection came from my port?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. Even though the site looks clean, it’s been in for months. The infectious disease team recommends removing it to clear the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about that. What if I need access later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MR venogram. Your jugular and SVC are open, so future access is possible. The subclavian veins are blocked, but we have options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to remove the port tomorrow. Surgery team will do it. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? And what about my warfarin? I’m on it for my SVC clot history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop warfarin the night before, restart it after. You’re not on heparin because of your HIT history, so it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re prepping for port removal today. How’s your headache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better since I started the sumatriptan. Still some nausea, but less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The sumatriptan is helping confirm it’s migraines. We’ll keep it as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The port was removed successfully. The tip culture will help confirm the infection source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt a fever last night. Was that from the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a mild spike is common after removal. You’re afebrile now, which is good. We’re waiting on the chamber swab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The swab from the port chamber grew Bacillus again, plus a little staph. Confirms it was the infection source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics and removing it should fix it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ll finish a three-week course of levofloxacin. We’ll monitor for recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I fell last night. Just caught my foot in the sheets. Hit my left knee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let me check it. Any pain, swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, on the inside. It’s swollen a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get an X-ray to be safe. No red flags, but better to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: X-ray shows mild arthritis and a small fluid collection, but no fracture. We’ll ice it and give pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I still walk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with support. We’ll put you on fall precautions. Try not to get up alone at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped, so we gave a unit of blood yesterday. It’s holding steady now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m always anemic. From malabsorption. But thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting up a hematology follow-up to check for other causes, like immune issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures are negative. That’s a great sign—the treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my lungs? The X-ray still shows pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s improving. Radiologically, it lags behind clinical improvement. You’re not coughing or spiking fevers, which is what matters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count dipped, likely from the prior antibiotics. It’s rising now that we switched to levofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely. But we’ll keep monitoring and follow up with hematology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been afebrile for days, headaches are controlled, and nausea is better. We’re thinking about discharge in a couple days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that. But I’m worried about pain control at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on a written Dilaudid taper—1.5 tablets three times a day for three days, then step down. Your PCP will help manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last chest X-ray shows stable pneumonia—still there but not worse. Infectious disease agrees you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: INR is 2.8—perfect for your clotting risk. You’ll restart your warfarin schedule and keep up with lab checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing discharge. You’ll finish levofloxacin for two more days, take sumatriptan as needed, and follow up with your PCP tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anxiety? I stopped Celexa because of nightmares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry recommends restarting at a lower dose or trying something else. They’ve sent info to your therapist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better. Scared of hospitals, but you’ve been kind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. You’re strong—managing a lot. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge: vitals stable, no fever, pain controlled. You’re good to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so relieved. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Remember: finish antibiotics, take sumatriptan early for migraines, and follow up with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if I have chest pain, trouble breathing, or high fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve got this. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I've been reviewing why you came in. You've been having abdominal pain, nausea, chest pain, and eye swelling—is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. The belly pain and vomiting have gotten worse over the last two weeks. I think it might be from restarting methotrexate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. Methotrexate can sometimes cause nausea and stomach upset. We also saw your CT scan—it didn’t show a bowel obstruction or blood clot in your neck, which we were worried about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I was scared it was my Crohn’s acting up again or another blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your Crohn’s doesn’t seem to be flaring—no diarrhea or bleeding. But your abdomen is tender, and you hadn’t passed gas in 24 hours when you arrived, so we’re watching closely for pseudo-obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pseudo-obstruction? What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s when the bowel acts blocked, but there’s no physical obstruction. It can happen after surgeries or with certain medications. We’ll keep you NPO for now and give IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the chest pain? It wakes me up at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ECG was normal, and your troponins are negative, so it’s unlikely to be your heart. It might be from straining when you vomit or gas buildup. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eyes were swollen. That’s gone now, but I had a weird noise in my ear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The eye swelling resolved, which is reassuring. The ear thing and the lung changes on your CT are a bit unclear. But your ANCA test was negative, so it’s probably not vasculitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lung changes? What kind of changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There are some small nodules and hazy spots in your lungs. They’ve been there before, and a pulmonologist reviewed them—they don’t look like infection or cancer. We’ll follow with X-rays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. Can I at least get my Dilaudid on schedule? I need it every few hours for the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started your usual IV Dilaudid, Benadryl, and diazepam as needed. We’ll keep it consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your belly is more distended today, and you’re still nauseated. We’re going to place an NG tube to help decompress your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An NG tube? I hate those. It’s so uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s not pleasant, but it will help reduce the pressure and nausea. We’ll make sure it’s placed correctly with an X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, if it helps. How much fluid came out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Over 2.5 liters already. That’s a lot, and it confirms your bowel isn’t moving things through properly. But no obstruction on imaging—this supports pseudo-obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a real blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not a physical one. Your bowel just isn’t contracting well. We’ll keep the NG tube in for a few days and let your gut rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat X-rays show no change—still no obstruction. The NG tube is working. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but the pain is a bit better. Can I try sipping water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to make sure your bowel is ready. We’ll wait until your nausea improves and the NG output decreases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back negative, so we’re stopping the Cipro. The initial test showed bacteria, but it wasn’t a true infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried about a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No need. Your symptoms are from your gut, not your bladder. We’re also stopping methotrexate for now—it might be contributing to your nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I restart it later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discuss it with your GI doctor. Given your reaction, they might adjust the dose or switch meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your NG output has decreased, and you’re less bloated. We’re going to try removing the tube and start clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. I pulled it out once yesterday, but then I vomited and they put it back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. This time, we’ll go slow—sips of water, then broth. If you keep it down, we’ll advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the clear liquids well. Today, we’ll try soft solids—applesauce, toast, maybe some Ensure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hungry. Can I have more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s not rush. Your gut has been through a lot. We’ll build up slowly to avoid setbacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you passed gas and had a small bowel movement. That means your gut is waking up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Finally! I was starting to worry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Me too. We’ll keep advancing your diet. You’re on track to go home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been tolerating soft foods well. No vomiting, pain is controlled with oral meds. We’re thinking discharge in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my lung nodules? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pulmonologist says they’re stable and likely not serious. No signs of infection or cancer. Just follow up with chest X-rays as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye swelling and ear noise?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The eye swelling resolved on its own. The ear thing doesn’t seem linked to anything serious. If it persists, see ENT as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’re on your regular pain meds by mouth, eating soft foods, and your abdomen is soft. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—Dilaudid, tramadol, oxazepam, Pepogest, Slomag. We’re restarting bupropion too, since you stopped it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And methotrexate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off for now. Talk to your GI doctor before restarting. We’ll send a note to them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. You’re stable, pain is controlled, and you’re tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop severe pain, can’t keep food down, run a fever, or stop passing gas, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your PCP in a week, GI doctor to discuss methotrexate, and pulmonology for chest X-rays. We’ll send all the records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel much better. Still a little tired, but the pain is way down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your body’s been through a lot. Keep resting, eat small meals, and take your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad this is over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with abdominal pain and vomiting after an abdominal massage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was sudden—projectile vomiting. I’ve had this before, but it scared me this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your vitals show a fast heart rate and slightly high blood pressure, which makes sense with pain. We’ve placed an NG tube to help decompress your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I actually placed it myself in the ER. It brought up about 250 cc. Does that mean it’s working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a good sign. It means we’re draining fluid and air. We’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now and give fluids through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I’m worried—could this be another bowel obstruction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our main concern. We did a KUB X-ray, and it shows dilated bowel loops, but no clear signs of a mechanical blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not blocked? But why am I so bloated and in pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of Crohn’s and pseudoobstruction, this looks more like your gut isn’t moving properly—what we call an ileus or pseudoobstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? I was just here a week ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re watching you closely. Surgery and GI have been consulted, and they agree with this approach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying to reduce my Dilaudid at home. I don’t want to rely on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll manage your pain with IV Dilaudid and Valium, as you’ve had before, but we’ll keep it as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your labs. Your kidney function was a bit off on admission—creatinine was 1.2—but it’s improved to 0.9 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because I was dehydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely pre-renal. IV fluids are helping. Your hemoglobin is low at 9.3, but it’s stable—consistent with your known iron deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my white count? I’ve had low counts before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s 4.4 now—was lower last night. Hematology has seen you before and says this can happen during hospital stays and isn’t always a concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CT scan results. No sign of small bowel obstruction. Your colon is dilated, but there’s no transition point—so likely pseudoobstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the NG tube? Is it in the right place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s in the distal esophagus, not the stomach. We need to reposition it so it can drain better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we do that now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nurse will help adjust it. We’ll confirm with an X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried to place a PICC line yesterday for better IV access, but we couldn’t advance the wire due to vein blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Because of my SVC issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. So we placed a midline in your left arm instead. It’s shorter but should work for fluids and meds during this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows the NG tube is still not quite in the stomach. The side port is at the GE junction. We may need to reposition it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s frustrating. Why won’t it stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your anatomy is complex from surgeries. We’ll keep adjusting until it’s right. The good news is your bowels are starting to decompress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having some diarrhea this morning—normal for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s actually a good sign. It means your gut is starting to move again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows slight improvement—less distension in your colon. We’re heading in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try sipping water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to see more bowel activity. We’ll try an enema today to help stimulate movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you passed stool after the enema yesterday. That’s a big step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit better. Can we remove the NG tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check an X-ray first. If your stomach stays decompressed, we can consider removing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows the NG tube is now in the stomach. But since you’re improving, we’re going to try removing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I hate having it in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight—no nausea or vomiting. We’re going to start you on clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with broth and see how you tolerate it. Small sips at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve kept down clear liquids. Today, we’ll advance you to a soft diet—mashed potatoes, applesauce, things like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really hungry. Can I have more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have to be cautious. Your gut is still recovering. Let’s see how you do today, then maybe more tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated the soft diet well. No vomiting. Your labs are stable. We’re making good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep this up, likely in a few days. We want to make sure you can eat and keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative—no infection. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a low-grade fever the other night. Was that just from stress?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your chest X-ray showed a chronic opacity in your right lung, but no new pneumonia. It’s likely stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The NG tube was replaced yesterday because it got dislodged, but we’ve removed it again today since you’re doing so well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even notice. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on a regular diet since yesterday—how’s your stomach feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. No pain, no vomiting. Just mild bloating, but that’s normal for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made it through the night with no issues. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust that call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried palliative care for pain—they suggested subcutaneous hydromorphone, but it didn’t help much. So we’re sticking with IV for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just need something that works. The pain is exhausting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture grew coagulase-negative staph. It’s likely a contaminant, but we’ll watch for fever or UTI symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had line infections with that bug before. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, we’re cautious, but this is likely from the Foley. We won’t treat unless you develop symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was low yesterday—3.5. We gave replacement, and it’s now 4.0. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Probably from not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. As we advance your diet, it should stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your latest X-ray shows the bowel is starting to move. The distention is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Can I try eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we’ll move to soft foods. We’ll also switch pain control to oral hydromorphone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some broth and felt okay. No nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll advance to a soft diet. Also, we’re adding misoprostol to help stimulate bowel movement, especially while you’re on pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken that before. Any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some cramping, but it should help overall. Take it with your pain meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—eating soft foods, pain controlled with oral meds. We’ll remove the NG tube today if you continue to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Please! I’m ready to be rid of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: NG tube is out. You kept down a sandwich and had no pain. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if things stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. My daughter’s wedding is next week—I really want to be home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still doing well. We’ll finalize your discharge plan. You’ll go home on oral hydromorphone for pain, diazepam for anxiety or nausea, and continue cipro and flagyl for the Crohn’s flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fondaparinux for my blood clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that daily. No changes. Also keep taking levothyroxine, omeprazole, and citalopram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about iron? My levels are always low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held off on iron supplements while your bowels were active. Your GI doctor will reassess that in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable, white count still low but unchanged. We’re comfortable discharging you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so relieved. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’ve tolerated a regular diet, pain is manageable with oral meds, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. What’s the follow-up plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment with Dr. Evans, your GI specialist, in five days. Call if you have worsening pain, fever, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my arm swells again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same thing—call or go to ER. Keep up with the fondaparinux and watch for bleeding, since it’s a blood thinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening and helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still some discomfort, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your discharge instructions are ready. Continue all meds as discussed, hydrate, eat as tolerated, and follow up with GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You came in last night with abdominal pain, fever, and shaking. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I woke up around 1 a.m. with a fever—up to 101—and then started shivering badly by 2 a.m. My left lower belly pain came back, worse than before, and I vomited twice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And does this pain feel like your previous episodes of bowel obstruction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly the same. I’ve been more bloated lately too. I haven’t had a bowel movement in a day, but I am passing gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The CT scan shows no bowel obstruction, but there’s a known narrowing at your ileal-colonic connection, and some new areas of thickening that may just be muscle spasms. We’re treating this as a Crohn’s flare with possible infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not another blockage? But why the fever and shaking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think the inflammation from Crohn’s may have let bacteria into the area, causing the fever. We’ve started antibiotics—Flagyl, ceftriaxone, and Levaquin—to cover that possibility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had an NG tube placed last night. Is that still needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. It’s helping to decompress your stomach since you’re nauseous and distended. We’ll check X-rays to make sure it’s in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray shows your NG tube was too high earlier, but we’ve adjusted it. It’s now sitting in your stomach, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense—I felt like it wasn’t helping at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about your IV access because of your history. We’re going to place a central line in your neck so we can give antibiotics and fluids safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had trouble with lines before. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll use ultrasound to guide it, and you’ll get light sedation. It’s the best way to ensure we can deliver your meds reliably.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The central line was placed yesterday. How are you feeling? Still in pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bloated and sore. The pain meds help a little, but I’m anxious too—being in the hospital brings back bad memories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve continued your citalopram and are using diazepam when needed for anxiety. We’ll keep the environment calm and give you space when you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative—no bloodstream infection. Stool tests also ruled out C. diff and other pathogens. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely Crohn’s then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. But we still need to check the narrowing in your bowel. We’re planning a colonoscopy tomorrow with possible dilation if it’s tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt? I’m nervous about the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under moderate sedation—fentanyl and Versed—so you’ll be very relaxed and won’t feel much. We’ll monitor you closely the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had the colonoscopy this morning. We found inflammation and narrowing at the anastomosis site. We took biopsies and dilated the stricture with a balloon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it go well? Was there bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it went smoothly. There was a small amount of bleeding after dilation, but it stopped on its own. The biopsies will confirm the extent of inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the biopsies—how long to get results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A few days. But based on what we saw, it looks like active Crohn’s inflammation, especially at the connection site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your white count has improved, and your kidney function is recovering. Your creatinine was 1.1 on admission but is now 0.5—great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so dehydrated before. I’m glad that’s better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re giving you fluids by mouth now, which is helping. We’re also starting rifaximin for bacterial overgrowth, which can worsen bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My right arm is swelling up. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking it. You have a history of SVC narrowing, so we’re doing an ultrasound to rule out a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the ultrasound showed no acute clot. The swelling is likely due to your chronic vein narrowing. We’ll use warm compresses and elevation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s already feeling a bit better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try advancing your diet today—starting with clear liquids. How’s your nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I think I can try some broth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on liquids. We’re removing the NG tube today since you’re not vomiting and your belly is less distended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I hated that tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy results are back. They show chronic active inflammation at the anastomosis with gastric metaplasia—consistent with Crohn’s. There’s also mild colitis higher up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s still active, even with my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, which is why you had this flare. We’ll continue the antibiotics and rifaximin, and your GI doctor wants you to follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now on a full soft diet and walking regularly. Your pain is much better—we’re switching from IV to oral Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about staying on IV meds too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also started IV iron for your anemia. You’ve been deficient for a while, and this will help your energy and healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired. I hope this helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows persistent but stable bowel dilation. No free air, which means no perforation. You’re healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing? I’ve noticed some spots on my chest X-rays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The patchy areas are chronic—likely old inflammation or bronchiectasis. No pneumonia or new fluid. Your lungs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had some increased nausea last night. The X-ray showed slightly worse bowel dilation, but we think it’s due to temporary slowing. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt bloated again. But I’m not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold off on the NG tube for now. Just rest your bowel for a few hours and we’ll try liquids again later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’re improving again. The last X-ray shows no free air and stable findings. We’re confident you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep tolerating food and staying pain-free, likely in the next two days. We’ll finalize your discharge plan tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re off IV meds, eating regular food, and your labs are stable. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue cipro, metronidazole, and now add rifaximin. We’re giving you a 14-day supply of oral Dilaudid and Valium for pain and anxiety, to taper as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your GI doctor in two weeks. Also follow up with your PCP about the Valium taper and your iron levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re discharged. Keep taking your meds, rest, and call if you develop fever, severe pain, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge instructions include stopping oxazepam and metaxalone. They’re not needed anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure to update my list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using the lidocaine patch for any localized pain. It’s safe with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve found it helpful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Someone will bring your prescriptions and discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Enjoy being home, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send a summary to your PCP and GI doctor so they’re up to date.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep taking your levothyroxine and citalopram as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t missed those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Stay consistent. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with worsening abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… it’s been terrible. The pain is constant, worse than last time. I’ve been vomiting bile, and I haven’t passed gas in over a day. My stomach is so swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were just discharged a week ago with similar symptoms. We’ve reviewed your history—Crohn’s, multiple surgeries, and bowel obstructions. We’ve placed an NG tube to help with the vomiting and decompress your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts when they put that tube in. And I’m scared—this keeps happening. Is something seriously wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The X-ray shows no complete blockage, but your symptoms suggest a partial obstruction, likely due to Crohn’s inflammation. We’re not seeing free air, so no perforation. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on cipro, flagyl, and rifaximin before. Should I keep those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing those to treat any infection and reduce gut inflammation. We’ll also keep the NG tube for now to help your bowel rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show low potassium—2.9. We’re giving supplements. This is likely from the NG tube suctioning stomach fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if not corrected. We’re replacing it carefully. As your NG output decreases, your potassium should stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your NG tube came out overnight. We replaced it this morning. We noticed you pulled it—was it uncomfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It makes me gag. I just wanted it out for a minute. I didn’t think…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand it’s uncomfortable. But removing it can make nausea and pain worse. Let’s work together—tell us when it’s bothering you, and we’ll adjust carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need to place a central line today. Your veins are tough to access, and we need reliable IV access for antibiotics and nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not again… I’ve had so many. Last time it was so painful. And I get anxious—being stuck, lying still…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know this is hard. We’ll give sedation and monitor you closely. The radiologist will use ultrasound to guide it. We’ll go slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed the line successfully through your left neck vein. It’s in the right spot. You did well during the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you… I was so scared. I almost couldn’t do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a low-grade fever the last two days. We added vancomycin to your antibiotics in case the line is infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the line infected? Should it be taken out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Blood cultures are negative so far. But since the fever came back when we stopped vancomycin, we suspect the line. We may need to replace it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The NG tube isn’t draining well. The X-ray shows it’s stuck in your esophagus. We’ll need to reposition it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? This is so frustrating. Can’t I just eat something small?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard. But your bowel isn’t moving well. If we try food too soon, it could worsen the blockage. We’ll reposition the tube to help it drain properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube is now in your stomach and draining. We also saw mild interstitial edema on the chest X-ray—likely from fluid shifts. It’s not severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I passed gas this morning. Does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign! It means your bowel is starting to wake up. We’ll keep monitoring. We might try a small sip of water later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try removing the NG tube for a few days. If you keep it down, we can start a liquid diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I hope I can keep it out. But what if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch closely. If nausea returns, we may need to reinsert it. But we’ll support you either way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You started vomiting again last night. We’ve reinserted the NG tube. It’s not a failure—it’s part of managing this condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I’m never going to get better. This is never-ending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. This is chronic and complex. But we’re making progress—your pain is a bit more controlled, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re replacing your central line today. The old one likely caused the fevers. The new one will go in a slightly different spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More procedures… I’m so tired of this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But this should help stop the fevers. We’ll use sedation again. You’ve handled these well before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new line is in. Your temperature has been normal since yesterday. That’s a good sign the infection source is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit better. Can I try eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids tomorrow. Slow and steady. Your bowel needs time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated broth and juice. We’re advancing to soft foods—applesauce, mashed potatoes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so hungry. But I’m scared it’ll hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. If pain increases, we’ll pause. But this is a big step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium is normal now. We’re stopping supplements. This is thanks to less NG drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I hate IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had to place another central line. The last one shifted. But it’s in now, and we’ll keep it monitored.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why does this keep happening? Am I just not healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not about healing. Your anatomy is complex—narrowed veins, scar tissue. It makes access hard. But we’re adapting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a small bowel movement yesterday. That’s excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was small, but I’m glad. Does this mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. We want you to tolerate a full diet and control pain with oral meds before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting to reduce your IV Dilaudid. We’ll switch to pills and taper slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared the pain will come back. I need that IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage it carefully. You’ve been on high doses, and we need to avoid dependence. We’ll adjust based on your comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your anxiety has been high. The acute pain team suggests restarting citalopram. It may help with both mood and pain perception.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on that before. It helped a little. Okay, I’ll try it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You passed gas again and kept down a soft meal. We’re making progress. We’ll keep the NG tube out and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have pain, but it’s less sharp. I think I can manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Hemoglobin is low at 7.2, but we’re not transfusing—you’ve had chronic anemia. We’ll follow up with GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tired all the time. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Also from chronic illness, poor nutrition, and the stress on your body. We’ll work on optimizing everything outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge in a few days. You’ll go home on oral Dilaudid, Valium taper, and continue antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about being home. What if I get sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set up close follow-up with your GI doctor. And you have our number for urgent concerns. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off the NG tube for three days, eating soft foods, and pain is manageable with oral meds. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s been so hard, but I feel like I can breathe again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge plan. Continue cipro, flagyl, and rifaximin. Take Dilaudid only as needed. And slowly taper Valium—don’t stop suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fondaparinux for my clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stop that. Hematology said three months was enough, and you’ve completed it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep my appointments. And call if things get bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve worked hard. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in with abdominal pain and neck swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The pain in my belly is like my past Crohn’s flares. And my neck felt so tight, like I was wearing a turtleneck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history, we’re concerned about a flare-up. We’ve placed a nasogastric tube to help decompress your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s uncomfortable, but I know it helps. I’ve had this before. I just worry you’ll think I’m only here for pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe you. Your symptoms are real. We’re treating this as a Crohn’s flare. We’ve started IV fluids and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My veins are bad though—always hard to get access. I had a femoral line tried in the ER but it failed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. A specialist placed a central line in your right neck under ultrasound guidance. It’s in the internal jugular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was it safe? I have SVC syndrome—veins are narrow. I had angioplasty before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. The line is in, but we’ll monitor. We’re avoiding heparin because of your HIT history—using saline flushes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. And the neck swelling—is it related to my veins?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re ordering an MRV to check your SVC and neck veins. We want to rule out a clot or worsening blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray shows some distention but no clear obstruction. Bowel sounds are slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not a full blockage? That’s good. But the pain is still bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No obstruction on CT either. We think it’s inflammation from Crohn’s. You’re on IV Dilaudid for pain and ciprofloxacin for infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRV is back. It shows complete chronic occlusion of your SVC and both brachiocephalic veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that why my face swelled? Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that likely caused the swelling. But you’ve developed good collateral veins—alternate pathways. Vascular surgery says no procedure needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s stable? I’m relieved. But what about my line in the neck?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it. Given your vein issues, we may need to move it later if it stops working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your current neck line is leaking from one port. We’re going to exchange it over the wire to a new one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I need sedation. I get very anxious with procedures, especially with men around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll use Versed and fentanyl, and ensure female staff are present. Your comfort is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The line exchange was successful. The new one is in the distal SVC. But your abdominal X-ray shows worsening obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel bloated. Is this going to turn into a full blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re managing it with the NG tube and bowel rest. Surgery doesn’t recommend surgery now. We’re hopeful it will improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a fever last night. My neck line site is red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you spiked a fever to 103.8. There’s redness at the site. We’re starting Vancomycin for a possible line infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the line is working, right? I need it for meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It infuses, but we can’t draw blood from it. That’s concerning. We plan to move it tomorrow under sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried to place a new line on the left side, but the veins are blocked. We had to re-site on the right neck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it working now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only one port draws blood. The others may be clotted. A chest X-ray suggests it might be in a collateral vein. We may need another change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve moved the line to your right groin. The neck line wasn’t functional. This femoral line is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: In my leg? That’s new. Is it safe long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’ll switch to a tunneled line later so you can go home on antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still anxious. Can I have something for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve lowered your diazepam dose because you were very sleepy. We can give oxazepam instead—less sedating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures and line tip were negative, but we’re continuing Vancomycin for 14 days due to high suspicion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I feel better. Fever’s gone. Can’t I stop early?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like you to finish. We’re placing a tunneled femoral line so you can get IV antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a tunneled line in your right groin. The left side was blocked. This one should stay secure for your Vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. How long do I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fourteen days total. You’ve had nine so far. But we’ll monitor—your counts are low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tunneled line came out accidentally. It’s no longer in the tunnel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no! Does that mean I have to stay longer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been fever-free for 48 hours and have had nine days of antibiotics. We discussed with you—discharge is safe with close follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about infection coming back. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever, chills, redness at any site. Come back immediately if that happens. You’ll get blood tests and cultures in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal pain has improved. You’re passing gas and tolerating soft foods. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. I was scared it would turn into a full obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tethering from scar tissue is still there, but not blocking. We’ll keep you on ciprofloxacin and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my anemia? My ferritin was low before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low at 8.6. We’ll follow up with your PCP. Iron deficiency is likely, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re doing much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. But what about pain at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get Dilaudid 4 mg—take one every three hours as needed. Don’t hesitate to use it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for anxiety?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oxazepam 15 mg twice daily as needed. We’re also restarting your citalopram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about future hospital stays. It’s so hard with my veins and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend a team meeting before any future admission—doctors, nurses, social work—to plan together with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would help so much. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send all instructions and prescriptions. Follow up with GI, vascular, and your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re removing the femoral line since it’s no longer tunneled. You’ll go home without a line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll watch for any signs of infection and come back if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve done well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the vascular surgery team. I understand you've been having some swelling in your neck and arms again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been getting worse over the last few days. It’s like the last time—swelling, headaches, blurry vision, especially when I lie back or lift my arms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds consistent with your SVC syndrome. We’re concerned the vein might be narrowing again. We’ll start with some imaging to check the blood flow in your neck veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time they did an ultrasound. Is that what you’re planning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve ordered a limited neck ultrasound to look at your internal jugular veins. That’ll help us see if they’re open and flowing properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the ultrasound shows both your internal jugular veins are patent and compressible. No clots there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I still so swollen then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The blockage might be further down, in the superior vena cava itself. We’re planning a venogram tomorrow to get a detailed look at that area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they try to open it during the test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if we see a narrowing, we’ll attempt a venoplasty or stent placement. But we’ll know more once we see the images.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just worried it won’t work again, like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. We’ll do our best. In the meantime, we’re also checking on your Crohn’s symptoms—you mentioned nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been nauseous. I think my Crohn’s is flaring again. My stomach’s been tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI has been consulted. They’ll evaluate you and make sure we’re not missing an obstruction or ileus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to take you down for the venogram. It’s a procedure where we inject dye into your veins and take X-rays to see the blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember this from before. Is it safe with my allergies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your allergies, especially to iodine-based contrast. We’ll use a low-risk agent and monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well during the procedure. We found significant obstruction in your SVC, but unfortunately, the stent placement wasn’t successful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted cardiothoracic surgery. You may need an open surgical bypass. They’ll set up a future date for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds serious. Is it safe after all my other surgeries?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s complex, but they’ll evaluate your full history. For now, we’ll manage your symptoms and plan the next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also got your blood culture results back. One came back with coagulase-negative staph and Enterococcus faecium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that an infection? I’ve had line infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started you on IV antibiotics just in case, but you’ve been afebrile and your white count is normal. It’s likely a contaminant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re stopping the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discontinuing them. No need to treat if it’s not a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray to check your Crohn’s symptoms. The first one was hard to read, but today’s shows distended colon loops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like ileus—slowed bowel movement—common with Crohn’s flares. No surgical obstruction seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more treatment for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI cleared you. We’ll manage nausea with medication and let your bowel rest. Most improve with time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures showed no growth. Confirms the earlier result was likely contamination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were too, but you’re stable. Your neck swelling is still there, but not worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Crohn’s symptoms are a little better. Less nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep supporting you until discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? What about the SVC blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The venogram confirmed the obstruction, but we couldn’t fix it. Surgery is the next step—we’ll schedule that as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
