conversation_lines.text: And my medications? I was on a lot before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve simplified them. You’ll continue levothyroxine, citalopram, and pain meds as needed. We added Cipro in case your Crohn’s flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the contrast dye from the test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Drink plenty of fluids—about 2 liters today—to help flush it out. Avoid metformin for two days, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bandage at the procedure site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remove the pressure bandage tonight, use a clean band-aid. Keep it dry—no showering for now. Watch for bruising or lumps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go up and down stairs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Limit stair climbing today. No lifting over 10 pounds for three days. Rest as much as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see cardiothoracic surgery to plan the bypass. GI follow-up in a few weeks. Call us if swelling worsens or you develop fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better knowing what’s next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. Take care, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team doctors. I understand you’ve been having facial swelling, headaches, and nausea again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been getting worse over the last few days. Especially when I lie back or lift my arms. My neck feels so tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds consistent with your SVC syndrome. Your last procedure didn’t fully resolve the narrowing in your superior vena cava, and we think it’s gotten tighter again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now? Last time they couldn’t place the stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because the blockage was too tight for a stent, we’ve scheduled you for surgery today. We’ll open the SVC and use a patch to widen it, along with removing the clot in your right subclavian vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? That sounds serious. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a major procedure, but necessary. The vascular and cardiothoracic teams will be working together. We’ve reviewed your history, including your HIT, so we’ll use fondaparinux instead of heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I trust you. I just want this swelling to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, it’s Dr. Lee again. The surgery went well. You had a SVC endarterectomy and a bovine pericardial patch placed. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you… I feel groggy, but my head doesn’t hurt as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ve extubated you, and you’re on a ventilator no longer. We’re watching your vitals closely in the ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you in the ICU for a few days, then move you to the VICU. You’ll start on fondaparinux for blood thinning and metoprolol for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your chest X-ray shows no pneumothorax, and your chest tubes were removed. The right upper lobe opacity is improving—likely atelectasis from surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m breathing easier. But I feel a little anxious being in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve restarted your diazepam and benadryl for anxiety. The chronic pain team also recommended morphine elixir—it’s helping with your comfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw your X-ray. There’s a small pleural effusion and some mediastinal widening. It could be post-op changes, but we’re watching closely for bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It’s common after this type of surgery. We’ll repeat imaging if needed. Your blood cultures were negative—no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray shows mild distention. Could be ileus, but we’re not concerned yet. You’re still tolerating food okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been bloated, but I’m eating. I did have some blood in my stool yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. Your C. diff test was negative, so it’s likely from your Crohn’s. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan because you had pain in your left groin. It showed contrast leaking from your line and a small hematoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no—does that mean it has to come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we removed the line. You don’t need it anymore, and it’s safer to avoid further bleeding. The hematoma is small and should absorb on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My pain’s better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped a bit during the transfusion yesterday. You had a reaction—severe left lower quadrant pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, sharp pain. But it went away after they stopped the transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it was related to the line issue, not the blood itself. You’re now anemic, so we gave you Epogen under the skin and oral lasix to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your levels are stabilizing. We’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your hemoglobin is up to 26.5%. You’re doing well. Physical therapy saw you and says you can walk independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We’ll discharge you with pain and anxiety meds, fondaparinux, and a follow-up with your PCP in four days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about driving or lifting. My sternum feels tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to follow sternal precautions for 10 weeks—no lifting over 10 pounds, no pushing or pulling. And no driving for at least four weeks, especially on narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about showering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can shower—just let water run over the incision. No baths for six weeks. Call us if you see redness, drainage, fever, or sudden swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge today. Your facial swelling is much improved, and you’re tolerating a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Here’s your discharge medication list. Fondaparinux daily, metoprolol twice a day, morphine for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The morphine elixir has helped a lot. Can I keep using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as needed. But your PCP will reassess in four days. We’ve also added ranitidine for stomach protection and docusate for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Crohn’s symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re managing that conservatively. Continue your usual meds. If diarrhea or bleeding worsens, call your gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I feel anxious at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the diazepam or diphenhydramine as prescribed. And don’t hesitate to call if anything feels off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I watch for blood in my stool again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Occasional blood can happen with Crohn’s, but if it’s heavy or persistent, get it checked. Your recent guaiac-positive stools weren’t from a serious bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. I’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, wear your surgical bra and avoid sleeping on your stomach. It helps protect your sternum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the mend. We’re discharging you in good condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Just glad this is behind me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. Rest, follow the instructions, and call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’re all set to go home with home services for support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team doctors. I understand you came in with a fever and chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up at 3 a.m. with a high fever—up to 103. It’s down a bit now, but I still feel awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned right-sided chest pain and chills. Any shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only when I move or take a deep breath. It’s been there since I left the hospital last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check your lungs and run some tests. Given your recent surgery, we need to rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had fevers before after surgeries. But this one feels different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re taking it seriously. We’ve ordered blood work and a chest X-ray. We’ll also do an ultrasound on your right arm because of the swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My fingers were numb earlier, but that’s better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That could be related to circulation. We’ll monitor that. Let’s get your vitals checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. White blood cell count is a bit low at 3.9, and your hemoglobin is 7.4, which is down from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Should I get a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it closely. No transfusion needed right now. Your electrolytes are off too—low calcium and magnesium. We’ll give supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always run low on those. My Crohn’s makes it hard to absorb nutrients.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep adjusting your IV fluids and supplements. Now, the ultrasound showed a clot in your right basilic vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another clot? But I’m on blood thinners!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but because of your HIT history, we’re using fondaparinux instead of heparin. This clot is in a superficial vein, so we’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it go away on its own?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, with the blood thinner. We’re more concerned about your chest. The X-ray shows some lingering changes in your right lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re starting you on IV antibiotics—vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam—just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to a lot of antibiotics. Are these safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we checked your allergies. These are safe for you. We’ll watch for any reaction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your leg ultrasound showed no DVTs. Both legs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about clots spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. But your arms are more concerning. We’re planning a CT scan to check your graft and lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to contrast. Won’t that be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll pre-medicate you to reduce the risk. It’s important we see what’s going on in your chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is done. There’s a small increase in fluid around your heart, but the graft looks patent and not infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the fluid dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately. It’s likely reactive. But we’re watching it. The lung shows more inflammation in the right upper lobe—consistent with infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it is pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. We’ll continue IV antibiotics and switch to oral later. We also found a small retained catheter fragment in your left chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should that come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s not causing issues. We’ll note it for future procedures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fever has come down. You’ve been afebrile for 12 hours now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a good sign. We’ll keep the antibiotics going and monitor your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried to place a PICC line for easier access, but your veins are too damaged. We had to use a temporary sheath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve always been hard to stick. It’s frustrating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. The radiologist noted extensive blockages and collaterals. We’ll manage with what we have.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT confirmed the lung infection is improving with treatment. The graft remains open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart fluid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but stable. No signs of infection in the graft. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been fever-free for over 48 hours. We’re ready to send you home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the oral antibiotic—levofloxacin—for two weeks. Take pain meds as needed. Watch for fever, redness at incisions, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood thinner?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue fondaparinux daily for a month. We’ll follow up with your PCP in four days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad this is behind me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Call us if anything changes. Rest and take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you've been having a tough few days. Can you tell me what brought you in tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I woke up three days ago with a high fever, chills, and headache. Then I started having bloody diarrhea and cramping on the right side—same as my Crohn’s flares before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned vomiting too, which caused pain at your sternotomy site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the dry heaving was so bad it made my chest hurt. My PCP said I should come in, so I went to my local ER first, then got transferred here for vascular and GI evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We’ve reviewed your history—Crohn’s, multiple surgeries, SVC repair, and HIT. You’re on fondaparinux, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 7.5 mg daily. I’ve been on it since my last hospitalization for HIT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll continue that, but we need to be cautious with the bleeding from your diarrhea. Vascular surgery will weigh in, but for now, we’re treating this as a possible Crohn’s flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I haven’t had bleeding with flares before, but maybe the anticoagulant is making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s a real possibility. Your labs show elevated CRP and ESR—both markers of inflammation—which supports a flare. But we’ve ruled out infections so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the pneumonia I was being treated for? I’m on day eight of levofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your chest X-ray shows the same right upper lobe changes as before—no new infection. So we think your pneumonia is resolving. The ciprofloxacin we’re starting will cover any lingering concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. My stomach is still so sore. Can we do something for the nausea and pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. You’ve already had IV hydromorphone and promethazine. We’ve placed an NG tube to help with the vomiting and gastric pressure. We’ll keep those meds going for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate IVs. My access is terrible—I’ve had failed lines before. Is there another way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Your chart notes multiple failed attempts. We’ll do our best, but if we lose access, we may need to switch to oral or rectal meds. The team is already planning for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back—no C. diff, no Salmonella, Shigella, or parasites. Blood cultures are negative too. That supports this being a Crohn’s flare, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection? That’s good. But why the fever and bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fever and CRP elevation are likely from gut inflammation. The bleeding could be from active colitis, possibly worsened by the anticoagulant. We’re starting ciprofloxacin and metronidazole to reduce inflammation and cover any subtle infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried steroids before—they made me crazy. I can’t do that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. GI recommended avoiding steroids due to your anxiety. That’s why we’re using these antibiotics—they can help with flares in patients like you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried to get a CT to look for strictures or abscesses, but we couldn’t secure IV access for contrast. Given your history of SBOs, it would’ve helped, but we’ll have to rely on clinical judgment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry. I know I’m hard to treat. My veins have been ruined for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This isn’t your fault. We’re doing everything we can. The KUB showed no obstruction, and you’re passing stool, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your IV just failed. We tried to restart it, but no success. The team discussed switching to oral hydromorphone and rectal promethazine. How do you feel about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Honestly, I’d prefer that. The IV pumps keep failing, and I feel worse when they stop working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch you to 8 mg oral hydromorphone every 4–6 hours and rectal Phenergan every 4–6 hours as needed. We’d like you to stay overnight to make sure you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but being here is really triggering my PTSD. I feel safer at home. Can I go if I promise to come back if I get worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Hospitalizations are hard for you. We discussed this with your husband and the attending. If you understand the risks—like severe bleeding or infection—we can discharge you early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do. I’ll take the meds as prescribed and call my PCP tomorrow. I’ll come back right away if I spike a fever or bleed more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll prepare your discharge. You’ll continue fondaparinux, levothyroxine, and citalopram. New meds are ciprofloxacin twice daily, metronidazole three times daily, oral Dilaudid, and rectal Phenergan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the diazepam? I’ve been taking it for anxiety and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll take one 5 mg tablet every four hours as needed. But please don’t mix it with the Dilaudid unless you’re awake and supervised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my anemia? My hemoglobin was low before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable—8.3 g/dL, slightly down but not concerning. We’ll monitor it at your follow-up. No transfusion needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m scared to leave, but I’m more scared to stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. Your safety is our priority. We’ll give you clear instructions and a direct number to call. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. You’ve taken two doses of oral meds—how’s the pain and nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The oral Dilaudid works faster than I expected. Nausea is much improved with the suppository.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember: finish all antibiotics, take your vitamins, and call your PCP within five days. Return immediately if you have high fever, dizziness, or heavy bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening and not pushing me to stay longer. I feel respected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be okay. I just need to be home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have the discharge papers ready in 15 minutes. Rest until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your NG tube can be removed now that you’re not vomiting. We’ll do that before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Please. It’s uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get it out right away. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I can finally breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Take it slow at home. Hydrate, rest, and follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you soon, hopefully in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will remove the NG tube now and go over your meds one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call us anytime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re discharged. Go home and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Finally. I’m so grateful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re feeling better. Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because of abdominal pain and distention. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I woke up last night with sharp pain and a lot of bloating. It felt like my old bowel obstructions. I’ve had Crohn’s for years and multiple surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were here two days ago with similar symptoms. The CT scan shows your colon is very distended with air and stool, but no blockage. This looks like an ileus—your bowel isn’t moving properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not another obstruction? That’s a relief. But why is this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history of Crohn’s and many abdominal surgeries, your bowel motility can be unpredictable. We’ll manage this conservatively—no food for now, IV fluids, and we’ll keep the NG tube to help decompress your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I placed the NG tube myself in the ER. It helps, but it’s uncomfortable. Will I need it long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it until your bowels start moving again. Once you pass gas or have a bowel movement, we can consider removing it and slowly restart your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been feeling a bit short of breath. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray, and there’s some consolidation in your right lung. It could be pneumonia or from aspiration. We’ll start antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Aspiration? I did vomit a little last night. But I’m not running a fever now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain it. Even without fever, we treat it because of your medical history. We’ll use levofloxacin instead of cipro, since you’re allergic to many antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have a long list. I’m also on fondaparinux for my HIT history. Will you continue that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll keep your home dose for blood clot prevention, especially since you’re not moving much right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your white blood cell count is low, and you’re mildly anemic. We’re watching that. Any gas or bowel movement yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I passed some gas last night, but no bowel movement. The bloating is still there, but maybe a little less?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Passing gas means your bowel is starting to wake up. We’ll keep the NG tube for now but may try a Gastrografin enema tomorrow to help move things along.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An enema? I’ve had those before. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be uncomfortable, but we’ll go slow. It helps us see if there’s a blockage and can also stimulate the bowel. The CT didn’t show a stricture, so we’re hopeful it’s just stool slowing things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Gastrografin enema was stopped early—you were getting uncomfortable, and the contrast only reached the descending colon. It looks like stool impaction is holding things up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a stricture from Crohn’s? That’s good. Can we do something to clear the stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO for now and let the Gastrografin work. It can act as a laxative. We’ll also keep the NG tube to suction to keep your stomach decompressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really tired. My labs showed low white count—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count has been dropping, but your blood cultures are negative. No infection is growing. It may be related to your Crohn’s or medications. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your chest X-ray shows the pneumonia is stable. But we’re still concerned because the right upper lobe opacity hasn’t improved. We’re continuing levofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I read one report said tuberculosis is possible. Is that true?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiologist mentioned it as a possibility because of the chronic appearance, but there’s no evidence you have symptoms of TB. Your PCP will follow up after discharge to decide if more testing is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’m also worried about IV access. I’ve had line infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a PICC line in your right leg vein under ultrasound guidance. It’s secure and ready to use. This avoids using your arm veins, which are compromised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel safer knowing it’s in a new spot. How’s my belly doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a small bowel movement this morning! That’s a big step. We’ll try removing the NG tube later if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! Can I try sipping water then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once the NG is out and you’re not nauseated, we’ll start clear liquids and advance slowly. Your gastroenterologist recommends continuing cipro and flagyl for your Crohn’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight—no nausea, passed gas again, and your abdomen is less distended. We’re removing the NG tube now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. I can finally breathe easier without it. Can I eat real food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids and soft foods. Given your short bowel syndrome, we’ll go slow to avoid overwhelming your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My anxiety’s been worse being in the hospital. Can I have my oxazepam? I lost my pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll prescribe a replacement. We know your PTSD makes hospital stays harder. We’ll keep your anxiety meds available as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two soft bowel movements and tolerated a full diet. Your lungs are clear, and vitals are stable. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue fondaparinux, levothyroxine, and sertraline. For pain, hydromorphone as needed. Promethazine for nausea, oxazepam for anxiety, and Nascobal nasal spray weekly for B12.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The levofloxacin is complete—five days. Your pneumonia is resolving. Your gastroenterologist will decide if you need cipro and flagyl longer as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your PCP and gastroenterologist soon. They’ll review the lung findings and your Crohn’s management. Call us if you have fever, severe pain, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m glad this wasn’t another surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. Your ileus resolved with conservative care, and your pneumonia improved with antibiotics. You’ve done really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable, and you walked to the lounge without issues. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel so much better. I’ll take it easy and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember to take your meds, stay hydrated, and reach out if anything changes. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take care and get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I definitely will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge nurse will go over your prescriptions and instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. You’ve come a long way in just over a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels like it. I’m just grateful it wasn’t worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your resilience helps. Keep listening to your body and following up with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having a lot of abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started a few days ago. I had right flank pain and thought I passed a kidney stone. I went to urgent care and they gave me Cipro and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. But then the pain came back, and you had nausea and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And my belly got really distended. I couldn’t keep anything down. I flew here because I knew I’d need help with my Crohn’s history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was a good call. Given your history of surgeries and ileus, we need to be careful. We’ve done a CT scan and an X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did it show? Is it a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No surgical blockage. But your colon is very distended. It looks like a colonic ileus — your colon has slowed down or stopped moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? But I haven’t changed my meds much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be from the extra pain meds you took for the flank pain. Opioids can slow the gut, especially in someone with Crohn’s and prior ileus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. So what do we do now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a nasogastric tube to decompress your stomach and rest your bowel. You’ll be NPO — nothing by mouth for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The NG tube again? It’s uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s not pleasant, but it helps relieve the pressure and nausea. We’ll keep it as short as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my right flank pain — could it be a UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test showed blood and some bacteria. We started you on Cipro, but we’ll wait for culture results to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. The NG tube is draining well. We’re giving you IV fluids and monitoring your belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any bowel sounds yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still quiet, but that’s expected early on. We’ll encourage walking to help stimulate your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying to walk a little. My heart’s been racing — is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from dehydration, pain, or anxiety. It’s improving, so we’re watching it. Your thyroid is stable on levothyroxine, so that’s not the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The urine culture came back. It’s E. coli, but it’s resistant to Cipro. So we’re switching you to Macrobid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so Cipro won’t work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the bacteria is resistant. But Macrobid should work well for your UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No growth so far, which is good. That means the infection likely hasn’t spread to your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another X-ray this morning. The NG tube is in good position, and there’s no worsening of the distention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we try sipping water yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to see some bowel activity first. We’ll listen again later and check if you’ve passed gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using the oxazepam for anxiety. It helps, but I’m still tense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Being in the hospital brings up past trauma. We’ll keep supporting you and keep your anxiety meds going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news — you passed gas last night, and your abdomen is less distended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s a good sign, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it means your bowel is starting to wake up. We’ll try a clear liquid diet today and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the NG tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll clamp it and see if you feel okay. If you don’t vomit, we can remove it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on clear liquids. No nausea or pain. We’re going to remove the NG tube now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. I hated that thing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance you to a regular diet tomorrow if this continues. Your pain is better — we’re switching from IV to oral Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can take pills now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll keep your anti-nausea meds on hand just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been eating regular food all day with no issues. That’s a big step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. Your UTI is being treated, and your blood counts are stable, though still on the lower side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My white count was low again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s consistent with your history. You’ve had this before, and it’s not dropping further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The team reviewed your case. You’re ready for discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Macrobid for the UTI, take Dilaudid for pain as needed, and use anti-nausea meds if required.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also adding Pyridium for bladder discomfort — it turns your urine orange, but that’s normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue levothyroxine, amlodipine, and fondaparinux. And oxazepam for anxiety as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still don’t take naltrexone — it gives me leg cramps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. Your gastroenterologist agrees it’s not essential. We’ll focus on what works for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, see your primary doctor in a week. And your urine culture was clear after the switch, so the antibiotic is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. All your labs are stable. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m so glad to be feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Remember to take the Macrobid for five days, and the Pyridium only for three.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever, severe pain, or can’t keep fluids down, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll follow up with my GI doctor about the ileus episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having worsening abdominal pain and vomiting for about a week. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been really bad. The pain is mostly on the right side, and it’s crampy. I’ve been vomiting almost every day. It feels just like my old ileus episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of Crohn’s and multiple abdominal surgeries, that’s definitely a concern. We’re going to keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth—to let your bowel rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’ve been so nauseous. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you IV fluids and anti-nausea medication. We’ll also place a nasogastric tube to help decompress your stomach and relieve the pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that tube from last time. It’s uncomfortable, but if it helps, I’ll do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure it’s placed correctly and monitor how you’re doing. We’ve already started your IV fluids and pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back, and it shows mixed bacterial flora, which likely means contamination from skin or genital area. So we don’t think you have a UTI this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried about another infection like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection so far. We’re more focused on your bowel function. We did an abdominal X-ray this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The NG tube needs to be advanced a bit—its side port is still in the esophagus. Once we fix that, it should work better. The bowel gas pattern is nonspecific, but there’s no clear obstruction. Some large bowel loops look borderline dilated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not blocked, but it’s not moving either?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It looks like paralytic ileus again—your bowel isn’t contracting properly. We’ll keep supporting you with fluids and the NG tube until it starts working again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: This keeps happening. I feel like I get an ileus every week now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s frustrating. Your history of Crohn’s and surgeries makes you prone to this. We’ll work on stabilizing you and then plan how to prevent future episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your labs. Your potassium is low, and your magnesium is also a bit off. We’re adding supplements to your IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be why I feel so weak and achy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, low potassium and magnesium can cause muscle aches and weakness. We’ll correct that, and you should start feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Any change with the bowel? I still don’t feel any movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still no bowel sounds or flatus, but we’re seeing small amounts of oral contrast moving into the rectum on imaging, so there’s some transit. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not completely shut down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not completely. It’s slow, but there’s some function. We’ll keep monitoring and hope to see improvement soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed something on your imaging and history—there may be a fistula between your bowel and genital tract. That’s not uncommon with Crohn’s and prior surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fistula? Like a connection that shouldn’t be there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It can cause pain, infections, or digestive issues. We’ll need to discuss this with your gastroenterologist for long-term management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds serious. Is it why I keep getting sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be contributing. It doesn’t explain everything, but it’s a factor we need to address. For now, we’re focused on getting your current episode under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your repeat urine culture today shows less than 10,000 organisms per ml. No infection. And your electrolytes are improving with supplementation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. And my stomach—still bloated, but maybe a little less?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the NG output has decreased, which means your bowel is starting to decompress. That’s a positive sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try sipping water yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips today. If you tolerate it and don’t vomit, we can slowly advance to clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on IV fluids for days. I really want to eat something soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we have to be careful. Your bowel needs time to wake up. Rushing it could trigger another ileus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your acid levels in the blood were off yesterday—we saw mild metabolic acidosis. But with fluids and electrolyte correction, it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from not eating or the vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Not eating, dehydration, and your body’s stress response all contribute. But it’s correcting now, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we noticed a compression of a vein, likely from prior surgery or scarring. It’s not causing issues now, but it’s something to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my circulation or clot risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on anticoagulants already, which helps. We’ll keep an eye on it, but no immediate action is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning! You’ve had a good night—no vomiting, sipped water well, and passed gas this morning. That’s a big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I didn’t even notice, but that’s great!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re going to remove the NG tube and start you on clear liquids. If you do well, you can go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home? That’s wonderful. What about my Crohn’s and the fistula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need follow-up with your GI doctor. They’ll evaluate the fistula and your overall Crohn’s management. We’ll send them all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the supplements? Do I keep taking potassium and magnesium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll send you home with oral supplements. Also continue your thyroid medication and anticoagulants as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling down lately with all these hospital visits. It’s hard to stay positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Your history includes depression and PTSD, and we don’t want to overlook that. Your primary can help connect you with support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d appreciate that. It’s not just the pain—it’s the constant worry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Healing isn’t just physical. We’ll make sure your care team knows to support you holistically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll go home today with instructions to advance your diet slowly and take your supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No NG tube, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s out. And you’ve tolerated sips well. Just avoid heavy meals for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor. If it’s severe with vomiting, come back to the ER. But I think you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up soon. We’ll make sure your records are sent over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid opioids? I think they made it worse last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, opioids can slow the bowel. We’ll recommend alternative pain management with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want to avoid another hospital stay if I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. With the right plan, we can help reduce how often this happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You can leave once the nurse reviews everything with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, eat small meals, and call if anything changes. Wishing you a smooth recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll follow up with my team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been having this pain in my right upper belly for weeks—like a balloon under my ribs. It comes and goes, and now it’s worse. It even goes into my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I vomit every other day, usually after climbing stairs with my grandkids. Not after eating, though. And I’ve had diarrhea for years—had six bowel movements today in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or breathing issues. But I’ve been really tired lately—barely getting out of bed. My depression’s been worse too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry to hear that. We’ll make sure to address that too. You mentioned past surgeries—can you tell me about those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had about 13 abdominal surgeries—mostly for blockages. I’ve had part of my colon removed, and I don’t have a gallbladder anymore. I also have Crohn’s disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We’ve reviewed your history. You’re also on several medications, including Dilaudid for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 6 mg every six hours as needed. I’ve been on that for a while now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll continue that for now. You also have a history of PTSD—anything we should know to help you feel more comfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’d prefer not to be alone with male staff if possible. It brings back bad memories from a past hospital experience.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll make sure the team is aware and respects that. We’ll always come in as a group when rounding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CT scan results back. It shows no acute issues—no blockages, gallstones, or pancreatitis. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not clear yet. The pain could be from adhesions or nerve irritation. There’s a small hiatal hernia, which might contribute to reflux, but it doesn’t fully explain your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had hernias before. Could it be blocking something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT didn’t show any obstruction. But we did see a few small gas pockets in your abdominal wall—likely from injections. Nothing concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your sodium was low—127—likely from not eating or drinking much and vomiting. We’re giving IV fluids to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if not treated, but we caught it early. Your levels are already improving. Your kidney function was a bit off too—creatinine was 1.2, but it’s likely due to dehydration. We expect it to return to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I haven’t been eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your sodium is now 135—much better. Kidney function is improving too. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but not as bad as when I came in. I think it’s closer to my usual baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We were going to do an MRE to check for adhesions, but it’s not available until later. Since your pain is better, would you prefer to go home and do it as an outpatient?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’d really like to go home. I’m feeling overwhelmed here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll arrange that. We’ll keep you on your regular Dilaudid for pain and continue your other meds, including citalopram for depression and fondaparinux for your vein condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a bit worried about managing the pain at home. Should I take the Dilaudid more often?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, stick to 6 mg every six hours as needed. We’re also giving you a small supply of 2 mg tablets in case you need something milder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the anxiety? Being in the hospital makes it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve prescribed diazepam—just one 5 mg tablet to take before your outpatient MRI if you feel anxious. It should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your morning labs look good. Sodium is 140, creatinine is 0.6—back to normal. Your pain is stable, and you’re alert and walking fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll discharge you. Continue your regular diet—gluten-free as before—and take your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the MRE?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll coordinate with your GI doctor to schedule it soon. Call your PCP or us if the pain worsens or you develop fever, vomiting, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening and helping me get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ve sent instructions to your husband, and follow-up appointments are set. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. I see you were just discharged a couple days ago, but now you’re back because of swelling in your legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. The swelling started in the hospital after my last admission. It’s been getting worse since I went home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. It’s bilateral, both legs, and it’s pitting—meaning when I press here, it leaves a dent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. It’s tender too, and I can’t even feel my pulses down there. I’m worried it’s my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a fair concern. That’s why we’re doing a full workup. Your primary care doctor checked a BNP, which came back elevated at 703. That suggests your heart might be under stress, so we’re looking into that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my last echo was okay, wasn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your echocardiogram today shows your heart is pumping well—ejection fraction is normal at 70%. But we did see moderate tricuspid regurgitation and mild pulmonary hypertension. That could contribute, but it doesn’t fully explain the swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not heart failure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not classic heart failure, no. The chest X-ray also showed no signs of fluid in the lungs. So we’re looking at other causes—like your liver, kidneys, or even your veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My liver? I know I have fatty liver, but it’s always been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the ultrasound today shows your liver blood vessels are open and there’s no blockage—so no Budd-Chiari syndrome. But we did see splenomegaly—your spleen is enlarged. That can happen with chronic liver congestion or other conditions, possibly related to your Crohn’s or portal hypertension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys? I had kidney issues last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. Your creatinine is normal at 0.8, and no protein in the urine. So it doesn’t look like nephrotic syndrome. Your kidneys seem okay this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about blood clots? With my SVC history and all the surgeries…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very valid concern. But you’re on fondaparinux for your SVC syndrome, and the Doppler ultrasound showed no clots in the liver or major veins. So we think it’s unlikely to be a new thrombosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not entirely sure yet. It could be a mix—maybe the tricuspid leak is contributing, or your body’s fluid balance is off due to your complex medical history. We’re going to start you on a diuretic—Lasix—to help your body get rid of the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will that make it better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. We’ll also keep you on a 2-liter fluid limit and low-sodium diet. Your weight was 98.8 kg today—we’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my abdominal pain? It’s still there, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your right upper quadrant pain is chronic, likely from adhesions or Crohn’s. It hasn’t worsened. You can keep using Dilaudid as needed, 6 mg every 6 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried they’d stop it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’ll continue what’s working. We also want to make sure your anxiety and PTSD are managed. I see you’ve had bad experiences in hospitals before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s hard being here. I feel safer when the whole team comes in together, and I’d prefer no male transporters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll make sure only female staff assist with transport, and we’ll round as a team. You can also take diazepam 5 mg at night if you’re feeling anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning look stable. Your potassium was a bit low yesterday—3.2—so we’re giving you supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the diuretic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Lasix can lower potassium, so we’re monitoring it. We also held your amlodipine temporarily—sometimes calcium channel blockers can worsen leg swelling, though it’s less likely since you’ve been on it for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, makes sense. How’s the swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve lost about 2 kg overnight—down to 96.8 kg. That’s a good sign the diuretic is working. The edema is still 2+, but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit lighter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re down to 94 kg—great progress. Your repeat labs are stable. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s fast. But what about the swelling? It’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s much improved. We’re sending you home on oral Lasix—40 mg daily—to continue the diuresis. Keep to 2 liters of fluid a day and a low-salt diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself daily. If you gain 3 pounds or more in a day, call your primary care doctor. Also, keep your follow-up with GI—they’ll schedule the MRE for your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anxiety meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue citalopram and can take diazepam 5 mg at night for the next two nights if needed. If anxiety flares, talk to your psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better knowing there’s a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up soon. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve had this right-sided abdominal pain and flank pain for a few days. It feels like my old bowel obstructions, but also different. I’ve been nauseous and threw up twice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned obstructions before—any recent changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I usually have many bowel movements a day, but I haven’t had any in two days. I feel bloated and distended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fevers or urinary symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a fever of 102 at home two days ago. I’ve also had back pain and burning when I pee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. You were started on azithromycin for possible pneumonia—any cough or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. Just the abdominal pain and nausea, which have gotten worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your CT scan. It shows some distention in the small intestine, but no complete blockage. This suggests a partial bowel obstruction, which fits with your history of Crohn’s and surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds familiar. But the pain feels different this time. Could it be something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re also considering a kidney infection because of your fever, back pain, and urinary symptoms. But the CT didn’t show kidney stones or swelling, so it’s less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did pass a kidney stone recently, but this pain is lower and more to the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps. We’ll keep monitoring. For now, we’re treating it as a partial obstruction. You’ll stay NPO—no food or drink by mouth—for a while to let your bowel rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about pain? It’s pretty severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you Dilaudid for pain. We know you’re used to it, so we’ll use it carefully. We’ll also give Zofran for nausea and IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been anxious in hospitals before—can I take my anxiety meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve prescribed Valium for anxiety while you’re here. You mentioned you usually take oxazepam—why did you run out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking it three times a day instead of twice. My PCP knows, but I didn’t have a refill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a short course of oxazepam twice daily until you see your doctor. We’ll also talk about the risks of combining it with Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show elevated CRP, which means inflammation. Your white count is normal, and kidney function is okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the bowel issue or infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be either. Your urine culture from outside grew E. coli, resistant to some antibiotics. Because of your allergies, we’re starting IV ampicillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had bad reactions to many antibiotics. Is ampicillin safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s not on your allergy list, and your infection is sensitive to it. We’ll watch you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. Did the fever mean pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray showed atelectasis—collapsed lung tissue—likely from shallow breathing due to pain. No pneumonia. Azithromycin was a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I haven’t been breathing deeply because of the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling an EGD and colonoscopy today to check for Crohn’s activity or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they help with the obstruction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not directly, but they’ll rule out inflammation or narrowing. You’ll stay NPO until after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the scope. The EGD and colonoscopy were normal—no active Crohn’s, no strictures. Biopsies were taken but likely normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? So it’s not a flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. This supports that your symptoms are from partial obstruction and possibly the UTI, not Crohn’s worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start eating now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids and advance as tolerated. If you do well, you might be ready to go home in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch you to oral ampicillin for a 10-day course. You’ll take it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a tapering dose of Dilaudid—start at 6 mg, then reduce over five days. This helps avoid withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about mixing it with my anxiety meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Valid concern. Together, they can increase sedation and affect breathing. Don’t drive or take other sedatives. Take them only as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your latest labs show improvement. White count is normal, CRP is coming down. No more fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood and urine cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood cultures showed no growth. The urine culture here was contaminated, but we’re confident based on the earlier result and your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotic is working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your pain is better, you’re passing gas, and tolerating food. All signs point to recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you today. You’ll continue ampicillin, the Dilaudid taper, and oxazepam for five days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you develop fever, severe pain, vomiting, or can’t keep food down. Also, if you feel overly sleepy or have trouble breathing, seek help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my husband can pick up the prescriptions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with ID. We’ve sent them to the pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have the discharge papers ready shortly. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because you had high fevers and confusion at your clinic. Can you tell me about your symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had fevers up to 104, a dry cough, and trouble breathing. I took Tylenol and the fever broke, but I felt confused when I got to the clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
